lead: A classifier cannot read raw text; it needs numbers. Text features turn each document into a vector over a fixed vocabulary. The bag-of-words model counts term occurrences and ignores order. TF-IDF multiplies each term frequency by a weight that is high for rare terms and low for common ones. These vectors feed spam filters, review classifiers and search ranking. The job is to build the vocabulary, compute counts and TF-IDF, and read the matrix that classifiers consume.
prereq: You need: Unit 1, tokenization and normalization — splitting text into terms and lowercasing them.

sections.h3: Vocabulary and the bag of words

blocks.text: The first step is a fixed vocabulary V. Tokenize each document, normalize case, optionally remove stop words and apply stemming. Collect every distinct term; each term gets a column. Build the vocabulary from training data only. Terms in test documents that are outside V are ignored or mapped to an unknown token. This keeps the vector size fixed and prevents information leakage.

In bag of words, document d becomes a vector c(d). The entry c(t,d) is the number of times term t occurs in d. Word order is lost, hence the name bag. Two documents with the same words in different order get the same vector. For topic and spam tasks this loss is often acceptable.
c(t,d) = number of occurrences of term t in document d
blocks.where: c(t,d) is the raw count; t is a vocabulary term; d is a document.

items: Binary bag of words sets c(t,d) = 1 if count > 0, else 0. Use it when presence matters more than repetition.
n-gram features use phrases such as not good or character trigrams. They capture local order. Keep n small, usually 1 to 3, to control vocabulary size.
Document length |d| is the total number of term occurrences after tokenization. For D1 = cricket bat ball, |d| = 3.

sections.h3: TF-IDF: term frequency and inverse document frequency

blocks.text: Raw counts over-weight long documents and common words such as the. TF-IDF fixes both. Term frequency is tf(t,d) = count(t,d) ÷ |d|. It is the share of document d taken by term t. Inverse document frequency is idf(t) = log₁₀(N ÷ df(t)). N is the number of documents. df(t) is the number of documents that contain t. A term in every document gets idf = log₁₀(1) = 0. The weight is w(t,d) = tf(t,d) × idf(t).

blocks.where: w(t,d) is the TF-IDF weight; count(t,d) is raw occurrences; |d| is total terms in d; N is number of documents; df(t) is document frequency of t. Log base 10 is common; base e or 2 changes scale, not ranking.

blocks.text: df counts documents, not total occurrences. If cricket appears five times in D1 and once in D2, df(cricket) = 2. Adding new documents changes df and idf for every term. Recompute the weights when the corpus changes. A term absent from d gets weight 0. The document-term matrix has rows for documents and columns for terms. It is sparse: most cells are zero. These vectors go to classifiers in 5.2.

Real corpora need small fixes. Add-one smoothing replaces N by N + 1 and df(t) by df(t) + 1 in the idf ratio. It keeps idf finite when df(t) is 0 or very small. It does not remove the zero weight of a term that appears in every document: if df(t) = N, then (N + 1) ÷ (N + 1) = 1 and log₁₀(1) = 0. Libraries add 1 to the whole idf, idf(t) = log₁₀((N + 1) ÷ (df(t) + 1)) + 1, so even an everywhere-term keeps a small non-zero weight. Sublinear (logarithmic) tf uses tf = 1 + log(count) instead of count ÷ |d|. A saturating tf uses tf = count ÷ (count + k), with k around 1; it caps the count without a logarithm. L2 normalization divides each document vector by √(Σ w²) so long documents do not dominate. These variants preserve relative term importance.

blocks.where: N is number of documents; df(t) is number of documents containing t. The +1 outside is a common library convention; it keeps a small non-zero weight when df(t) = N. Without the outside +1, a term in every document has idf = log₁₀(1) = 0.

items: Add-one smoothing: idf = log((N + 1) ÷ (df + 1)). It stays finite for df = 0 or small df, but still gives 0 when df = N.
Sublinear (logarithmic) tf: tf = 1 + log(count) when count > 0.
Saturating tf: tf = count ÷ (count + k), with k around 1. It caps the count without a logarithm.
L2 normalization: w ← w ÷ √(Σ w²) over terms in the document.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this term weighting or the vector space model. The output is a document-term matrix: rows are documents, columns are terms, cells are weights. In code, scikit-learn TfidfVectorizer does this, with smooth_idf and sublinear_tf options. For dense word vectors, see 5.5.

figure.caption: The idf row is high (0.48) for bat, stock and market, each found in only one document, and low (0.18) for cricket and ball, which appear in two. D3 is zero under the three cricket terms, so a classifier can separate the stock/market topic from the cricket one.

spec.title: TF-IDF worked example (log₁₀); columns: cricket, bat, ball, stock, market
spec.aria: A five-row table over the terms cricket, bat, ball, stock and market shows document frequency (2, 1, 2, 1, 1), the idf of each term (0.18, 0.48, 0.18, 0.48, 0.48), and the TF-IDF weight rows for D1, D2 and D3, where D3 is zero in all three cricket columns.

examples.question: Three documents are D1 = cricket bat ball; D2 = cricket ball; D3 = stock market. Build the vocabulary. Using tf(t,d) = count(t,d) ÷ |d| and idf(t) = log₁₀(N ÷ df(t)), compute the TF-IDF matrix rounded to two decimal places. N is the number of documents and df(t) is the number of documents containing t.
steps: Tokenize and list the vocabulary in this order: cricket, bat, ball, stock, market. N = 3 documents.

Count document frequencies: cricket is in D1 and D2, so df(cricket) = 2; bat is in D1, so df(bat) = 1; ball is in D1 and D2, so df(ball) = 2; stock is in D3, so df(stock) = 1; market is in D3, so df(market) = 1.
Compute idf values: idf(cricket) = log₁₀(3 ÷ 2) = log₁₀(1.5) = 0.1761; idf(bat) = log₁₀(3 ÷ 1) = 0.4771; idf(ball) = 0.1761; idf(stock) = 0.4771; idf(market) = 0.4771.
For D2, tf(cricket) = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5; tf(ball) = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5; other terms have tf = 0. Weights: cricket = 0.5 × 0.1761 = 0.0880 → 0.09; ball = 0.0880 → 0.09.
For D3, tf(stock) = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5; tf(market) = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5; other terms have tf = 0. Weights: stock = 0.5 × 0.4771 = 0.2386 → 0.24; market = 0.2386 → 0.24.
examples.check:
import math
docs = [['cricket','bat','ball'], ['cricket','ball'], ['stock','market']]
vocab = ['cricket','bat','ball','stock','market']
N = len(docs)
df = {t: sum(1 for d in docs if t in d) for t in vocab}
for d in docs:
    length = len(d)
    for t in vocab:
        c = d.count(t)
        tf = c / length
        idf = math.log10(N / df[t])
        w = tf * idf
        print(f'{w:.2f}')

traps: Using raw counts as TF-IDF. The tf part must be normalized by |d| in this definition, and then multiplied by idf.
Counting df as total occurrences. df(t) is the number of documents containing t, not the number of times t appears.
Forgetting that idf changes when documents are added. A weight computed on a small corpus is not valid on a larger one.
Treating a term in every document as important. Its idf is zero, so its TF-IDF weight is zero.
Building the vocabulary separately on training and test sets. The columns must match; unseen test terms need an unknown token or must be dropped.

quiz.q: In TF-IDF, what do N and df(t) mean?
quiz.a: N is the number of documents in the corpus. df(t) is the number of documents that contain term t; it is not the total occurrences of t.

quiz.q: Why does a term that appears in every document get idf = 0?
quiz.a: Its df equals N, so N ÷ df = 1 and log₁₀(1) = 0. The term cannot distinguish documents, so its TF-IDF weight is zero.

quiz.q: A document has length |d| = 4 and term t appears 2 times. N = 10 and df(t) = 5. Compute tf and TF-IDF using log₁₀.
Two documents contain the same words in different order. Their bag-of-words vectors are equal. What information is lost, and name one task where that hurts.
quiz.a: Word order is lost, so phrase meaning and negation can be lost. Sentiment analysis on a phrase where order changes meaning can fail; n-gram features reduce this loss.

quiz.q: Vocabulary is [a, b]. D1 has a twice and b zero, |D1| = 2. D2 has a once and b once, |D2| = 2. N = 2. Compute idf for a and b with log₁₀, and TF-IDF of b in D2.
Give one reason to use binary bag of words instead of raw counts.
quiz.a: Presence may matter more than repetition. A word repeated many times should not dominate, and binary features reduce document-length effects.

quiz.q: Why build the vocabulary on training data only?
quiz.a: Using test data leaks information and creates features unavailable at training time. Test terms outside the training vocabulary must be ignored or mapped to an unknown token; this keeps evaluation honest.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, TF-IDF features still appear in search ranking, spam filters and baseline classifiers; BM25 is a close relative. Large sparse matrices are stored in compressed sparse row format, and the hashing trick avoids storing a vocabulary by mapping terms to a fixed number of columns. Scikit-learn's TfidfVectorizer and HashingVectorizer are common starting points. Search next for BM25, feature hashing and sparse document-term matrices.
